title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers
authors: Leo Y. Li-Han, Chris Varghese, Elizabeth B. Habermann, Mark J. Truty, William R. G. Perry, Cornelius A. Thiels
abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) contain complementary diagnostic and laboratory information about patient health. However, irregularity, sparsity, heterogeneity, and incompleteness in documentation complicate EHR modeling. To address the problem, we introduce GraphBEAT (Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation over Time), a temporal graph representation learning framework that groups clinical events into time buckets and transforms observed features into patient-specific, temporally directed graphs to enable early risk stratification for gastrointestinal cancers. Each node in an EHR graph encodes feature identity, observed value, and temporal position of clinical events. A context-aware, time-decay message-passing mechanism models transitions between successive buckets, followed by multi-head attention pooling to generate patient-level representations. GraphBEAT was trained and evaluated on multi-site longitudinal diagnosis codes and laboratory tests to predict pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancer at 12-, 24-, and 36-month diagnostic lead times. In all experimental setups, GraphBEAT consistently outperformed baseline graph neural networks (GraphSAGE, GAT, and GCN) and sequence modeling approaches (Transformer and long short-term memory [LSTM]). GraphBEAT also required over 250x fewer floating-point operations per patient and over 20x fewer parameters than the Transformer and LSTM baselines. These results support GraphBEAT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach for cancer risk stratification from sparse, heterogeneous longitudinal health records.

infographic.key_insight: GraphBEAT turns irregular longitudinal EHR events into time-aware graphs, improving early cancer risk stratification with far lower compute than standard deep learning baselines.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help identify patients at higher risk of gastrointestinal cancers earlier using routinely collected diagnosis codes and lab tests.
method: Buckets EHR events over time to handle sparsity and irregular visit timing
Builds patient-specific directed graphs where nodes encode feature, value, and time
Uses time-decay message passing plus multi-head attention pooling for prediction
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained and tested on multi-site longitudinal diagnosis codes and laboratory tests, GraphBEAT outperformed GraphSAGE, GAT, GCN, Transformer, and LSTM for pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancer prediction at 12-, 24-, and 36-month lead times.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was shown on retrospective EHR data, so real-world generalization and prospective clinical utility still need validation.
infographic.paper_title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers

title: Developing an OMOP-Standardized Prostate Cancer Database and Improving Data Quality Using NLP and PSA-Based Algorithms
authors: Wang, J.; Jackson, J. C.; Garza, A.; Nalla, S.; Ninnemann, T.; Zhang, Y.; Kuo, Y.-F.
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate an Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership-(OMOP-) standardized prostate cancer database from the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) Epic Electronic Health Record (EHR) and improve data quality using natural language processing(NLP) and prostate-specific antigen-(PSA) based algorithms. Materials and MethodsWe built a data pipeline to transform UTMB Epic EHR data for patients identified through the Galveston Cancer Registry (2010-2021) into OMOP Common Data Model (CDM) v5.4. Data quality was assessed by comparing the OMOP-standardized data with Galveston Cancer Registry data using availability agreement, Cohens kappa and Intraclass Correlation Coefficient. NLP was used to extract PSA, Gleason score, and cancer stage from clinical text, and PSA-based algorithms were used to identify missing treatment and biochemical recurrence. ResultsWe extracted 815 analytic cases from UTMB EHR. Among them, 700 (85.9%) were complete and concordant with the cancer registry. PSA showed excellent value agreement. Structured Gleason score and stage data were sparse (n<20), but NLP greately improved capture. Treatment agreement was good compared with the cancer registry and improved slightly for radical prostatectomy after applying a PSA-based algorithm. Using PSA trajectories, we identified 60 cases of biochemical recurrence. DiscussionThe OMOP-standardized data from UTMB showed good agreement with the cancer registry. However, structured EHR fields incompletely captured diagnosis, pathology, and treatment details. NLP and PSA-based algorithms substantially improved data capture. Manual review also revealed errors in registry data, showing that OMOP-standardized EHR data can complement and help improve cancer registry quality. Conclusion: OMOP standardization combined with NLP and PSA-based algorithms improved prostate cancer data quality and research readiness. Lay SummaryElectronic health record (EHR) systems contain valuable long-term health information about cancer, but their use is limited by difficulties in data extraction, the lack of standard data formats, and missing information in structured fields. In this study, we built a data pipeline to convert EHR data into the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model, a widely used standard format that facilitates data sharing and collaborative research. To address missing data, we used natural language processing (NLP, a computational technique that enables computers to interpret human language) to extract prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, Gleason scores (a measure of cancer aggressiveness), and cancer stages from unstructured clinical notes. We also applied algorithms that track PSA blood trends over time to identify unrecorded cancer treatments and detect cancer recurrence. Comparing this database with a cancer registry demonstrated that standardized EHR records provide accurate clinical information and long-term follow-up. While structured EHR fields lacked key tumor characteristics, NLP dramatically improved their capture. Tracking PSA trends identified previously unrecorded treatments and flagged 60 potential cancer recurrences. Overall, combining standardized EHR formats with NLP and PSA-based algorithms creates a rich database to support real-world prostate cancer research.

infographic.key_insight: Standardizing prostate cancer EHR data to OMOP and adding NLP plus PSA-based rules materially improved missing diagnosis, pathology, and treatment information.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach can make routine EHR data more usable for prostate cancer research, registry validation, and outcomes tracking.
method: Converted UTMB Epic EHR prostate cancer records into OMOP CDM v5.4.
Used NLP to extract PSA, Gleason score, and cancer stage from clinical text.
Applied PSA-based algorithms to detect missing treatments and biochemical recurrence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The pipeline yielded 815 analytic cases, with 700 (85.9%) complete and concordant with the cancer registry; PSA agreement was excellent and NLP substantially improved sparse Gleason/stage capture.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a single-center retrospective dataset, so performance and data quality gains may not generalize without local validation and careful mapping of registry/EHR discrepancies.
infographic.paper_title: Developing an OMOP-Standardized Prostate Cancer Database and Improving Data Quality Using NLP and PSA-Based Algorithms

title: MedPAO-VL: Interpretable and Protocol-Compliant Agent for Structured Radiology Report Generation
authors: Shrish Shrinath Vaidya, Gowthamaan Palani, Minmini Selvam, Gokulraja Srinivasaraja, Ganapathy Krishnamurthi
abstract: Despite the remarkable generalization capabilities of Large Language Models, generating clinically accurate and structured radiology reports from medical images remains a significant challenge. Current end-to-end approaches function as black boxes, prone to factual hallucinations and generating ungrounded findings. This lack of reliability and failure to adhere to domain-specific structuring protocols, fundamentally limits their clinical utility. We present MedPAO-VL, a multimodal agent that shifts the paradigm from monolithic generation to explainable, iterative, protocol-compliant structured report generation. Unlike deterministic models, our plan-act-observe loop functions as a goal-oriented agent: it first perceives the Chest X-Ray through an explainable vision module designed to capture inherent diagnostic uncertainty, then iteratively refines the generated report by observing semantic discrepancies and self-correcting its generation for better alignment with visually detected clinical findings. Evaluation of our framework demonstrates that this agentic reasoning improves clinical correctness and completeness, achieving an expert-rated accuracy score of 3.5/5 and a structural score of 4.3/5. By prioritizing pathology specific explainability and iterative refinement over opaque end-to-end mapping, MedPAO-VL offers a transparent and clinically viable alternative for automated structured radiology report generation.

infographic.key_insight: MedPAO-VL replaces one-shot radiology report generation with an explainable plan-act-observe agent that iteratively corrects itself to improve structure and factual alignment.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach aims to make chest X-ray report generation more trustworthy, protocol-compliant, and clinically usable by reducing hallucinations and improving report completeness.
method: Perceives chest X-rays with an explainable vision module that models diagnostic uncertainty
Uses a plan-act-observe loop to detect semantic discrepancies and refine the report iteratively
Targets structured, protocol-compliant radiology report generation rather than free-form text
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports expert-rated performance of 3.5/5 for accuracy and 4.3/5 for structural quality.
infographic.watch_item: Promising results are from expert ratings in a specific chest X-ray setting, so broader validation and workflow testing are still needed before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: MedPAO-VL: Interpretable and Protocol-Compliant Agent for Structured Radiology Report Generation

title: Tool-Augmented Large Language Models for Reliable Medical Calculation from Patient Notes
authors: Yang Zhong, Ling Luo, Xuanlyu Zhu, Yanhua Wang, Yuanyuan Sun, Jian Wang
abstract: Medical calculators translate raw patient observations into clinically actionable values and scores. However, applying these calculators directly to free-form patient notes requires precise variable extraction combined with the exact execution of complex formulas, scoring rules, and output conventions. Relying solely on direct large language model (LLM) prompting is unreliable in this context, as rule recall, parameter extraction, arithmetic reasoning, and formatting become entangled within a single generative step. To address these limitations, we propose a tool-augmented LLM framework for reliable medical calculation from patient notes. The framework retrieves and structures calculator specifications, generates reusable executable tools, and uses a constrained extractor to map each patient note to calculator-ready inputs. The tools then perform deterministic calculation, separating clinical language understanding from rule execution and arithmetic. Evaluated on the MedCalc-Bench dataset, our method achieves 86.73% final-answer accuracy, outperforming the one-shot prompting and supervised fine tuning-only baselines by 24.0 and 17.27 percentage points. Ablation and error analyses show that these performance gains are primarily driven by rule-grounded tool synthesis and schema-constrained extraction, whereas remaining failures are concentrated in clinical-semantic extraction and benchmark-specific output contracts. By grounding calculator logic in executable tools, the proposed approach alleviates arithmetic hallucinations and improves the computational reliability of the final clinical outputs.

infographic.key_insight: A tool-augmented LLM pipeline can turn free-text patient notes into reliable medical calculator outputs by separating clinical variable extraction from deterministic formula execution.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve the consistency and trustworthiness of automated clinical scoring and calculation tasks when working with messy real-world notes.
method: Retrieve calculator specs and convert them into executable tools.
Use constrained extraction to map patient notes into calculator-ready inputs.
Run deterministic tool-based calculations instead of relying on the LLM to do the math and formatting.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MedCalc-Bench, the method reached 86.73% final-answer accuracy, beating one-shot prompting by 24.0 points and supervised fine-tuning-only baselines by 17.27 points.
infographic.watch_item: Remaining errors still cluster around clinical-semantic extraction and strict benchmark-specific output formatting, so deployment would need careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Tool-Augmented Large Language Models for Reliable Medical Calculation from Patient Notes

title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
authors: Boya Zhang, Yuanchao Ma, Jiageng Wu, Krittaphas Chaisutyakorn, Rodrigo Gameiro, Ahram Han
abstract: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information. To capture multilingual pain representations, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and adopt an ensemble strategy to improve performance. Ten clinicians across four languages validate the labels: the ensemble reaches macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 on pain relevance and pain presence and 92-100% accuracy on demographics, with inter-annotator $κ$ of 0.82-1.00. We release the WorldMedQA-Pain ensemble labels, the extraction pipeline, validation scripts, and clinician annotation sheets for publicly licensed corpora, providing a foundation for pain-centered clinical NLP and for studying pain documentation across languages and healthcare contexts.

infographic.key_insight: PAINT is a multilingual framework that standardizes how pain is identified and described across exams and real-world clinical texts in English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It could help clinical NLP systems better detect and structure pain documentation across languages, supporting more consistent symptom analysis and research.
method: Curated nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning medical licensing exams and clinical text
Built a structured schema for pain relevance, presence, location, descriptors, and demographics
Used LLMs with an ensemble strategy and clinician validation across four languages
infographic.evidence_signal: The ensemble achieved macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 for pain relevance and pain presence, 92-100% accuracy for demographics, and inter-annotator κ of 0.82-1.00.
infographic.watch_item: Results are strong on annotated corpora, but real-world deployment may still be limited by language-specific documentation styles, context dependence, and corpus licensing boundaries.
infographic.paper_title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts

title: Can GPT Be Used as an Alternative Prediction Model to Traditional Machine Learning and Neural Networks on Low-Volume Clinical Data?
authors: Bin Akter, S.; Akter, S.; Eisenberg, D.; Hill, C.; Lotvola, A.; Fresneda Fernandez, J.; Sarkar Pias, T.; Rafiqul Islam, M.; Islam, H.
abstract: Background and Objective: Early and reliable disease prediction from structured clinical data remains challenging when datasets are small, highly imbalanced, and contain limited positive disease cases. Conventional machine learning (ML) and deep learning approaches often struggle to capture clinically meaningful relationships under such low-data representation conditions due to weak statistical associations between features and prediction targets. This study proposes a clinically grounded GPT2-based table-to-text framework for disease prediction using structured healthcare datasets, motivated by the contextual reasoning capability of GPT models to better capture clinically meaningful relationships when statistical learning alone becomes insufficient due to limited data availability. Methods & Materials: Structured clinical records were transformed into physician-style textual descriptions and enriched through GPT4-generated medical paraphrasing to improve minority-class representation while preserving clinical meaning. Both the original and generated clinical texts were used to fine-tune a GPT2 model across four public healthcare datasets, including heart disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and thyroid cancer recurrence. Gradient-based explainable AI analysis was additionally incorporated to identify clinically important features influencing prediction outcomes. Results: The proposed framework demonstrated consistently strong predictive performance with average precision, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.96, 0.97, 0.96, and 0.96, respectively. The model achieved improved sensitivity, stronger generalization, and more stable predictive behavior compared with traditional ML, deep learning, transformer-based, and GAN-augmented approaches. Importantly, the framework consistently emphasized clinically meaningful variables even under severe class imbalance where conventional ML and neural network models often struggled. Conclusions: The proposed GPT2-based table-to-text framework provides a practical and clinically interpretable approach for disease prediction from limited structured healthcare data. By integrating contextual clinical reasoning with explainable prediction mechanisms, the framework demonstrates strong potential for early risk detection, transparent clinical decision support, and reliable deployment in real-world low-resource healthcare environments.

infographic.key_insight: A GPT2 table-to-text approach can outperform traditional ML and neural networks on small, imbalanced clinical datasets by leveraging contextual clinical reasoning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests a potential way to improve disease risk prediction from limited structured healthcare data while keeping outputs more clinically interpretable.
method: Converted structured patient records into physician-style text.
Used GPT4-generated paraphrasing to augment minority-class examples.
Fine-tuned GPT2 on four public healthcare datasets and applied gradient-based explainability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across heart disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and thyroid cancer recurrence datasets, the model reported average precision, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.96, 0.97, 0.96, and 0.96.
infographic.watch_item: The results are based on public low-volume datasets, so external validation and careful checks for synthetic-text bias are needed before real-world deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Can GPT Be Used as an Alternative Prediction Model to Traditional Machine Learning and Neural Networks on Low-Volume Clinical Data?

title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts
authors: Zhaoyu Fan, Bowen Han, Jincheng Ou, Yanwei Ren, Zehua He, Kaiyu Huang
abstract: Real-world studies (RWS) analyze routinely collected healthcare data, such as electronic health records and insurance claims, to estimate treatment effects, monitor safety, and identify risk factors outside randomized trials. Automating RWS with large language model agents is appealing but brittle: valid analyses depend on dataset-specific clinical semantics, including index dates, follow-up windows, patient/event-level units, and outcome boundaries that are often implicit in observational data. This leads to schema mismatches, temporal errors, inconsistent analytical granularity, and unsupported clinical claims. We present ProCARE, a profile-grounded framework that reformulates RWS automation as constrained compilation. ProCARE converts heterogeneous data profiles into Evidence Contracts specifying available variables, temporal attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits, and compiles study objectives into RWS-IR, a strongly typed intermediate representation for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks. Deterministic validation and localized repair then check and revise generated workflows across schema mapping, cohort construction, variable derivation, analysis, and interpretation. On 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks, ProCARE outperforms strong LLM-agent baselines in code executability, semantic consistency, and conclusion traceability, with automated violation diagnoses showing moderate-to-substantial agreement with blinded expert review.

infographic.key_insight: ProCARE turns real-world study automation into a constrained compilation problem by grounding LLM workflows in dataset-specific evidence contracts and a typed intermediate representation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It could make automated observational analyses from EHR and claims data more reliable by reducing schema mismatches, temporal mistakes, and unsupported clinical interpretations.
method: Builds profile-derived Evidence Contracts that describe variables, time attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits.
Compiles study goals into RWS-IR, a strongly typed format for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks.
Uses deterministic validation and localized repair to fix issues across schema mapping, cohort building, derivation, analysis, and interpretation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks, ProCARE outperformed strong LLM-agent baselines in executability, semantic consistency, and traceable conclusions, with automated violation diagnoses moderately to substantially matching blinded expert review.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on accurate dataset profiling and may still require careful human oversight when clinical semantics are incomplete or ambiguous.
infographic.paper_title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts

title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
authors: Ting Liu, Haoran Lai, HaobinChen, Ming Liu, S Kevin Zhou
abstract: Contrastive vision-language pre-training supports zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image-report pair in a batch as a negative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic incompatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not establish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We therefore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity distributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable student, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of $0.850$, compared with $0.837$ for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.

infographic.key_insight: SCCL-DT reduces false-negative supervision in chest X-ray contrastive learning by using adaptive, semantic-conflict-aware masking plus dual-rule teacher distillation for zero-shot diagnosis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve zero-shot chest X-ray triage support by making vision-language models better at recognizing shared findings across patients instead of over-penalizing similar cases.
method: Tracks image-report similarity with EMA statistics to set adaptive thresholds.
Hard-masks likely semantic conflicts before softmax, instead of treating all off-diagonal pairs as negatives.
Uses two teachers with OR and AND rules, then distills them into one student model.
infographic.evidence_signal: On five public chest X-ray benchmarks, the model reports a mean zero-shot AUC of 0.850 versus 0.837 for the strongest compared baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract notes that the online-mask audit only suggests finding agreement and does not prove clinical equivalence, so thresholding and masking may still be sensitive to dataset shift.
infographic.paper_title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis

title: The Federated Tumor Segmentation and Classification (FeTS++) Challenge
authors: Wenyi Tang, Carla Pitarch-Abaigar, Siddhesh Thakur, Verena Chung, Konstantinos Koukoutegos, Alexandros Karargyris
abstract: International challenges have become the standard for developing and benchmarking biomedical image analysis methods using centralized multi-institutional data. Federated learning (FL) describes a paradigm-shift on multi-institutional collaborations, where models are trained across institutions while their data are always retained locally. The Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge, first held in 2021, was the first challenge dedicated to FL in medical imaging and editions in 2022 and 2024 pushed the frontiers of real-world method validation. FeTS++ 2027 returns after a two-year gap with a substantially larger and more diverse cohort, and with the two "pluses" that name the challenge: an official classification task alongside segmentation, and a move of the infrastructure to NVIDIA FLARE (NVFlare). Built on the clinically acquired, multi-institutional multi-parametric MRI data of the BraTS 2025 Lighthouse challenge, FeTS++ spans gliomas and meningiomas across patient cohorts from institutions in North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, and focuses on ranking submitted methodological approaches according to their model utility and an efficiency-aware score. Task 1 asks participants to find the best strategy for aggregating knowledge from per-institution segmentation models, while Task 2 asks them to distinguish glioma from meningioma under the same federated protocol, in which the entity label is heavily confounded with the site of origin.

infographic.key_insight: FeTS++ 2027 expands federated medical imaging benchmarking by adding a classification task and a new FL infrastructure, while testing methods across more diverse multi-institutional brain tumor data.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It helps evaluate whether federated AI can generalize across hospitals without sharing patient data, with potential relevance for tumor segmentation and tumor-type differentiation workflows.
method: Federated training across institutions with data kept local
Task 1: aggregate per-site tumor segmentation models
Task 2: classify glioma vs meningioma under a site-confounded federated setup
infographic.evidence_signal: The challenge uses clinically acquired multi-parametric MRI from multiple regions worldwide and ranks submissions by model utility with an efficiency-aware score.
infographic.watch_item: Because tumor type is strongly confounded with site of origin, performance may reflect institution-specific patterns rather than true generalization if not carefully evaluated.
infographic.paper_title: The Federated Tumor Segmentation and Classification (FeTS++) Challenge

title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation
authors: Ziyang Song, Lia Shen, Yixuan Li, Qincheng Lu, Weihao Li, Haoran Xu
abstract: Biomedical language models (LMs) provide strong representations for clinical tasks, but they often fail to capture the hierarchical structure among medical concepts. This limitation is especially pronounced for rare and fine-grained clinical codes in long-tailed vocabularies, where hierarchy-agnostic LM representations become less informative as concept frequency decreases. We introduce Semantic Medical Identifier (SMI), a training-free framework for constructing ontology-grounded Semantic IDs and hierarchy-aware medical concept representations. For each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept, SMI defines its Semantic ID as the coarse-to-fine path through an expert-defined medical ontology. SMI then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the corresponding ontology levels to form hierarchy-aware medical concept representations that preserve coarse-to-fine clinical semantics. The base SMI uses uniform aggregation across ontology levels, while a level-weighted variant selects global level weights on validation data. Our theoretical analysis shows that SMI yields more informative medical concept representations than hierarchy-agnostic LM embeddings, particularly for rare and fine-grained clinical concepts. Experiments show that SMI captures meaningful hierarchical structure and improves clinical relation prediction. On MIMIC-IV, SMI improves mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction. On eICU, SMI yields more robust patient representations under cross-hospital distribution shift.

infographic.key_insight: SMI turns medical concept codes into ontology-based semantic paths and combines them with frozen biomedical embeddings to better capture hierarchy, especially for rare and fine-grained concepts.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve clinical prediction and recommendation systems by making representations of diagnoses, procedures, and medications more informative and robust across hospitals.
method: Build a Semantic ID for each concept using its coarse-to-fine path in a medical ontology.
Aggregate frozen biomedical LM embeddings across ontology levels to create hierarchy-aware concept representations.
Use either uniform weighting or validation-tuned level weights to emphasize more useful ontology levels.
infographic.evidence_signal: In experiments on MIMIC-IV and eICU, SMI improved mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, rare drug prediction, and robustness under cross-hospital shift.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and coverage of the expert-defined ontology, and the weighted variant requires validation data to tune level weights.
infographic.paper_title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation

title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining
authors: Joshua Placidi, Inigo Stibbe, Alfred J. Balston, Marek Rei, A. Aldo Faisal
abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models predict the next event token in patient trajectories: sequences of structured medical events. A typical pretraining strategy is to concatenate all trajectories into a global stream and sample token windows from it. This gives patients with longer sequences more training exposure and allows tokens to attend across patient boundaries. We argue that these choices create a misalignment between pretraining and downstream clinical tasks. To explore this, we investigate how the composition of pretraining sequences affects clinical prediction performance. Using the global-stream approach as a baseline, we propose alternative sequence composition methods that control how patient trajectories contribute to pretraining sequences. Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks, our best method improves macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, with relative gains of 9.3% in F1 and 2.7% in AUPRC under a fixed training recipe. We find that these gains generalize across four additional evaluation settings, including the INSPIRE and eICU-CRD datasets, with improvements in macro AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 score. Our results show that simply changing how EHR data are presented to the model during pretraining can improve downstream performance, without changing the model or collecting additional data.

infographic.key_insight: How patient EHR sequences are grouped during pretraining can meaningfully change foundation model performance, even without changing the model itself.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better sequence composition during EHR model pretraining may improve downstream clinical prediction tasks and support more reliable decision-support tools.
method: Compared a global-stream pretraining baseline with alternative ways of composing patient trajectories into training windows.
Evaluated the methods on four MIMIC-IV v2.2 clinical prediction tasks.
Tested whether gains carried over to four additional settings, including INSPIRE and eICU-CRD.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks, the best method improved macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, with gains also generalizing to four extra evaluation settings.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from retrospective benchmarks, so real-world benefit and robustness will still need external validation and careful implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining

title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift
authors: Sara Inácio, Hugo Proença, João C. Neves
abstract: Foundation models have shown significant potential across diverse fields and have been applied to medical imaging, but their robustness across patient populations remains unclear. In this work, we investigate foundation models' ability to generalize from adult to pediatric chest X-ray classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark to compare multiple foundation models under a common adult-to-pediatric evaluation setting while also analyzing the effect of adaptation depth. We harmonize VinDr-CXR and PediCXR into a five-label classification task and evaluate six foundation models and two CNN baselines. All models are adapted using adult data only and tested in both the in-domain and pediatric domains using linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. The benchmark reveals a clear and consistent trend: all models suffer a substantial performance degradation when transferred from adult to pediatric data, with drops exceeding 10 percentage points. While Macro-AUROC values reach approximately 92% on the adult test set, performance decreases to around 78% on the pediatric domain. Another important finding is that increasing the depth of adaptation does not significantly improve cross-population generalization. Moreover, strong in-domain performance does not translate into better performance on pediatric data.

infographic.key_insight: Chest X-ray foundation models trained on adult data lose substantial accuracy when applied to pediatric cases, and deeper adaptation does not reliably fix this domain shift.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Adult-to-child transfer in medical imaging may require pediatric-specific validation or retraining, because strong adult performance may not generalize to children.
method: Harmonized VinDr-CXR and PediCXR into a five-label chest X-ray classification task
Benchmarked six foundation models plus two CNN baselines
Compared linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning using adult data only
infographic.evidence_signal: Across in-domain and pediatric testing, Macro-AUROC fell from about 92% on adult data to about 78% on pediatric data, with drops exceeding 10 percentage points for all models.
infographic.watch_item: The results suggest that high adult test performance should not be assumed to indicate safe or reliable pediatric deployment without dedicated external validation.
infographic.paper_title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift

title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning
authors: Li-Ching Chen, Andrés Franco Valiente, Yuta Ishiyama, Zachary R. Chalmers, William Chen, Kelsey Natsuhara
abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.

infographic.key_insight: The study shows that reinforcement learning can improve a language model’s clinical reasoning in oncology by using partially verifiable, patient-specific rewards from real-world decision processes.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may help support more structured, sequential treatment planning for colon cancer when multiple reasonable choices exist under incomplete patient information.
method: Formulated colon cancer treatment planning as an interactive RL task under partial observability
Built process-aware rewards from real clinical records to guide information gathering and treatment selection
Optimized Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with GRPO and GDPO and evaluated reasoning alignment
infographic.evidence_signal: In the abstract, the GDPO-trained policy improved Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by 79.60% over the base Llama and surpassed GPT-5.2 by 18.82% in the same interactive environment.
infographic.watch_item: The environment is still a simulation of partially observed clinical decisions, so real-world deployment would need careful validation for safety, robustness, and clinician oversight.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning

title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
authors: Weichen Lyu, Chong Xia, Mingyu Dong, Long Xu, Shengjun Zhang, Yueqi Duan
abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.

infographic.key_insight: PhySGA combines an agentic planner, a physics-aware critic, and simulator actions to make 3D object composition more generalizable and interactive across rigid, articulated, and deformable objects.
infographic.clinical_relevance: While not a clinical tool, better physics-grounded 3D assembly can improve medical simulation, robotic manipulation, and digital training environments used in healthcare workflows.
method: Assembly Agent handles global step planning and coarse geometric/kinematic alignment.
Critic Agent diagnoses simulator state using contact dynamics and performs fine-grained closed-loop corrections.
Action Routers and a Self-Evolving Skill Library turn plans into simulator actions and reuse successful trial-and-error experience.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive experiments in Isaac Sim showing improvements in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality over existing methods.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulator-based, so real-world transfer and robustness to simulation mismatch remain important implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition

title: A Two-Level Clinical Novelty Prioritization Framework for Disease Trajectories Discovered from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
authors: Jin-Jia Zheng, Vincent S. Tseng
abstract: Graph-based analysis of electronic health records (EHRs) yields disease-trajectory catalogs, but structural support does not establish semantic novelty. We present a two-level framework to prioritize 99,527 branching motifs previously discovered by an upstream patient-disjoint, train-only MIMIC-IV v3.1 pipeline and frozen after validation-based catalog selection. The framework separates path-level and node-to-endpoint semantic sparsity from reliability-adjusted clinical priority. Three deterministic textualizations per motif or node-target pair were embedded with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 and calibrated against 166,972 pre-2023 PubMed references using mean top-20 cosine distance. Positive recombination occurred in 8.63% of motifs and had negligible effect on global ranking, whereas specificity and support/GNN reliability terms changed clinical-priority ordering. Robustness analyses across neighbor counts, templates, encoders, generic-label taxonomies, score settings, PrimeKG, and corrected density-based RND showed that broad ordering was more stable than hard top-k membership. A semantic-dose analysis did not support a monotonic relation between score and forecasting benefit after endpoint and token-count adjustment (1.96 days per SD; 95% CI, -0.75 to 4.68). In the frozen catalog-q90 high-semantic subgroup, branch-enhanced forecasting reduced conditional event-time MAE by 20.1 days (95% CI, 13.3-27.0) and sMAPE by 2.37 percentage points (95% CI, 1.81-2.93), while discrimination and endpoint-ranking differences were inconclusive. Corrected RND showed low tail agreement with the primary score (Spearman rho = 0.430; q90 Jaccard = 0.125) despite a similar aggregate timing association. These findings support representation-aware, uncertainty-aware literature-relative prioritization of discovered trajectories rather than causal discovery or clinician-adjudicated novelty.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a two-level framework that ranks EHR-discovered disease trajectories by both semantic novelty and clinical priority, rather than relying on structural support alone.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help researchers focus on the most potentially informative trajectory patterns for retrospective study and hypothesis generation, while avoiding overinterpretation of novelty as clinical causality.
method: Encoded three textual versions of each trajectory motif/node-target pair with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5.
Compared embeddings against 166,972 pre-2023 PubMed references using mean top-20 cosine distance to estimate semantic sparsity/novelty.
Combined novelty with reliability-adjusted priority signals and tested robustness across templates, encoders, taxonomies, and scoring settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the frozen high-semantic subgroup, branch-enhanced forecasting improved conditional event-time MAE by 20.1 days and sMAPE by 2.37 percentage points, but broader ranking stability and some downstream associations were mixed.
infographic.watch_item: The framework supports literature-relative prioritization, not causal discovery or clinician-adjudicated novelty, so its scores should not be treated as direct clinical guidance.
infographic.paper_title: A Two-Level Clinical Novelty Prioritization Framework for Disease Trajectories Discovered from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records

title: LightHybridNet: A Lightweight Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Efficient Multi-Label Ophthalmic Disease Classification in Imbalanced Fundus Images
authors: Hem Raj Dadral Najam Ul Hasan, Naveed Ejaz, Muhammad Aslam Jarwar
abstract: Eye diseases are a major global cause of blindness and vision impairment, highlighting the need for accurate and early diagnosis to prevent further deterioration. Despite advances in medical imaging, classifying retinal diseases from fundus images remains challenging due to the complexity and subtlety of visual features. This study aims to develop and validate LightHybridNet, a novel lightweight hybrid deep learning framework, to improve the classification of eye diseases from fundus images. The model incorporates architectural features, such as depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling mechanisms, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and robustness. To validate the model, the ODIR-5K dataset, comprising 8 disease categories, was used. To enhance image quality, pre-processing approaches were applied, including histogram equalisation, colour space conversion, and contrast adjustment, resulting in high-resolution images. Furthermore, image augmentation was employed to increase the dataset size, thereby improving the model's ability to generalise during training. The hybrid architecture helps the model concentrate on relevant image regions while capturing and integrating details at different scales, significantly improving classification performance. To evaluate its effectiveness, the model was compared with transfer-learning models. The results show that LightHybridNet outperforms the baselines, achieving a weighted F1-score of 91.51%, a macro AUC of 98.26%, and a Cohen's Kappa of 90.14% on the validation set. Furthermore, model interpretability was enhanced using explainable AI methods, including Grad-CAM, to identify and emphasise features influencing the decision-making process. LightHybridNet represents a promising advancement in automated ocular disease detection, offering improved diagnostic reliability for clinical use.

infographic.key_insight: LightHybridNet is a lightweight hybrid deep learning model that improved multi-label retinal disease classification from fundus images, especially in an imbalanced setting.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may support earlier and more reliable automated screening of ophthalmic disease from routine fundus imaging, with explainability features to help interpretation.
method: Used the ODIR-5K fundus image dataset with 8 disease categories.
Applied preprocessing including histogram equalisation, colour space conversion, and contrast adjustment.
Used augmentation and a hybrid architecture with depthwise separable convolutions, compound scaling, and Grad-CAM interpretability.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the validation set, LightHybridNet achieved a weighted F1-score of 91.51%, macro AUC of 98.26%, and Cohen's Kappa of 90.14%, outperforming transfer-learning baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was reported on a specific benchmark dataset, so external validation on other populations, devices, and clinical workflows is still needed before broad deployment.
infographic.paper_title: LightHybridNet: A Lightweight Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Efficient Multi-Label Ophthalmic Disease Classification in Imbalanced Fundus Images

title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation
authors: Rui Tang, Hongqiu Wang
abstract: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.

infographic.key_insight: MedHarnessBench shows that healthcare-specific runtime support can improve both task success and the quality of agent actions, not just final outcomes.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For healthcare AI systems, this benchmark helps distinguish whether failures come from the model, the tool/workflow harness, or their interaction, which is critical for safer deployment.
method: Defined the Medical Harness Protocol to separately score seven process dimensions in healthcare agent execution.
Built MedHarnessBench with 342 executable tasks spanning FHIR/EHR operations, admin interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools.
Tracked intervention traces to see whether runtime support was available, used, and carried into later behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors report more than 16,000 controlled task executions, with MedHarness improving terminal success, intermediate completion, and healthcare-specific process quality.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from benchmarked, controlled workflows, so real-world performance may differ when systems face messy clinical data, changing policies, or high-stakes edge cases.
infographic.paper_title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation

title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
authors: Zihao Zheng, Junyi Yao, Baichuan Li, Jiayu Long
abstract: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.

infographic.key_insight: Healthcare LLMs can look highly accurate on clean questions yet still fail badly when they must decide whether to answer, ask for clarification, abstain, or escalate under workflow uncertainty.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In patient-facing workflows, unreliable escalation can miss important safety triggers, so decision policies need evaluation beyond answer accuracy alone.
method: 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes built from 40 semantic seeds
Five controlled variants tested across four task classes and two surface forms
Compared five open-weight LLM configurations under ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE with a preset 5:1 missed-vs-unnecessary escalation cost
infographic.evidence_signal: Clean decision accuracy reached 0.97, but uncertainty-prompted models missed 32% to 97% of required escalations and one model fell from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict.
infographic.watch_item: The workflow-aware controller improved benchmark utility, but its rule detectors collapsed on paraphrased triggers, so real-world generalization remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures

title: Graph-Enhanced Disease Trajectory Discovery and Temporal Endpoint Forecasting from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
authors: Jin-Jia Zheng, Vincent S. Tseng
abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can reveal disease-progression structure, while useful forecasting requires leakage-controlled discovery, censor-aware outcomes, and inspectable trajectory evidence. We developed a graph-enhanced framework in MIMIC-IV v3.1 that splits patients before graph construction, learns train-only consecutive-admission transitions, and freezes endpoint-specific branching-motif policies selected on validation data. The final catalog contained 99,527 motifs, and a time-aware Transformer retrieved at most 24 patient-compatible motifs per endpoint through endpoint-specific cross-attention. Across five training seeds, micro-AUPRC increased from 0.9330 to 0.9357, while event-time MAE decreased from 676.9 to 657.7 days (reduction 19.2 days; 95% paired patient-cluster bootstrap CI, 13.8-24.8). Timing effects were heterogeneous: MAE worsened for events within 730 days but improved by 58.9 days for events occurring after 730 days. In an exploratory internal temporal split, branch conditioning reduced conditional event-time MAE by 26.9 days (95% CI, 23.0-30.8) without evidence of better micro-AUPRC. Corrected survival evaluation over the supported 0-2,555-day interval did not establish macro C-index or integrated Brier score superiority over a matched history-only discrete-hazard model. A directed, degree-matched GNN repair substantially improved unseen-edge discovery, yet replacing GNN-derived scores within fixed motif identities did not improve downstream forecasting. These results position branching motifs as structured trajectory context whose main value is long-range timing support rather than uniformly stronger endpoint discrimination, survival prediction, or causal explanation.

infographic.key_insight: Leakage-controlled branching motifs from longitudinal EHRs mainly improved long-range event-timing forecasts rather than overall endpoint discrimination.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This framework could help researchers build more interpretable disease trajectory models from EHRs, but it is not yet a basis for clinical decision-making.
method: Split patients before graph construction to prevent information leakage.
Learned train-only consecutive-admission transitions and selected endpoint-specific branching motifs on validation data.
Used a time-aware Transformer with endpoint-specific cross-attention to retrieve up to 24 patient-compatible motifs per endpoint.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five seeds, micro-AUPRC rose from 0.9330 to 0.9357 and event-time MAE fell from 676.9 to 657.7 days, with larger gains for events occurring after 730 days.
infographic.watch_item: The gains were selective, with no clear improvement in corrected survival metrics over a matched history-only model and limited benefit from replacing GNN-derived scores.
infographic.paper_title: Graph-Enhanced Disease Trajectory Discovery and Temporal Endpoint Forecasting from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records

title: HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
authors: Min Xiao, Jin Li, Shoujin Wang, Yeguang Zhen, Yishuo Li, Wenpeng Lu
abstract: Medication recommendation (MR) is critical for clinical decision support. While existing MR methods are mostly designed for single-center learning, where only one independent hospital is involved, multi-center MR with hospitals of different scales has become increasingly demanding in practice. In multi center settings, abundant data from large medical centers can improve recommendation performance for low-resource centers. Despite a few preliminary attempts on this task, two critical gaps remain. Gap 1: Existing multi-center methods fail to disentangle transferable cross-hospital clinical experience from hospital-specific prescribing patterns, limiting clinical feasibility and physician acceptance. Gap 2: They commonly overlook multi label safety constraints of MR, including drug-drug interaction risks and local formulary feasibility, which are essential for safe real-world deployment. To address these gaps, we propose HEM-Med, a novel hierarchical agentic memory framework for multi-center MR. To address Gap 1, we design a disentangled hierarchical memory module that builds patient-level medication context attribution records and disentangles them into cross hospital experience memory and hospital-specific residual memory. To address Gap 2, we introduce a safety-aware medication set generation module, which integrates dual-level experience retrieval with safety-aware set decoding to produce clinically relevant, safer, and locally adaptive medication recommendations. Experiments on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset show that HEM-Med outperforms representative transfer learning, LLM-based, and MR baselines in terms of both recommendation accuracy and safety.

infographic.key_insight: HEM-Med separates transferable cross-hospital prescribing experience from hospital-specific patterns, then uses safety-aware decoding to recommend medications more safely across multiple centers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help smaller hospitals benefit from large-center learning while better respecting local formulary constraints and reducing unsafe drug combinations.
method: Builds a hierarchical memory of patient medication context
Disentangles memory into cross-hospital experience and hospital-specific residuals
Uses safety-aware set generation with dual-level retrieval for medication recommendation
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset, where HEM-Med outperformed transfer learning, LLM-based, and other medication recommendation baselines on accuracy and safety.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is shown on one multi-center dataset, so broader validation is needed before assuming the same safety and generalization in other hospitals.
infographic.paper_title: HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
